comparison: Both evaluate the Notch signaling pathway's role in vm2 specification (C1, C2, C3, C5, C20-C28). OpenEval finds the evidence sufficient based on genetic screens, rescue experiments, and molecular characterization. Peer reviewers question whether the data demonstrate a 'partial fate switch' versus 'selective disruption of muscle arm growth program' and request additional fate markers, indicating uncertainty about the mechanistic interpretation.

Both address UNC-40 and MADD-2 as downstream effectors (C31-C43). OpenEval considers the expression patterns, rescue experiments, and genetic interactions as strong support. Peer reviewers' uncertainty about whether this represents postsynaptic specification versus a muscle differentiation program extends to the interpretation of these downstream targets.

Both evaluate molecular characterization of UNC-40/MADD-2 (C79-C85). OpenEval and peer reviewers agree on the quality of the molecular and genetic data. Peer reviewers' concerns focus on interpretation (muscle differentiation vs synapse specificity) rather than disputing the expression patterns and genetic interactions documented.

Both evaluate anatomical and developmental characterization of vm2 synapse formation (C6-C8, C44-C45, C53-C56). Both find this well-supported by EM reconstruction, fluorescence imaging, temporal analysis, and ablation experiments. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'an interesting muscle differentiation program' and accept the anatomical documentation.

Both address epithelial cell organization and presynaptic independence (C9-C10, C46-C49, C54-C56). Both find strong support for epithelial cells as organizers and neurons as dispensable for muscle arm development. Agreement on the anatomical and developmental relationships.

Both evaluate the organizational role of epithelial cells (C88-C91). Both support the model of non-neuronal cells organizing synapse development through muscle arm formation. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge 'the participation of the muscle cell in synapse development through muscle arm formation' and epithelial involvement.

Both evaluate molecular and phenotypic characterization of lin-12 alleles (C11-C12, C57-C60, C67-C71). OpenEval finds comprehensive support from mutation characterization, rescue experiments, and phenotypic analysis. Peer reviewers do not dispute the phenotypic data but express uncertainty about whether this represents fate change versus selective program disruption, requesting more fate markers.

Both evaluate functional consequences including calcium imaging and behavioral data (C13-C17, C61-C66). Both find this data supportive. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative functional validation; peer reviewers acknowledge this as part of documenting the muscle differentiation program and its role in circuit function.

Both address temporal requirements via temperature-shift experiments (C19, C72-C73). OpenEval finds clear support for L4-stage requirement independent of earlier roles. Peer reviewers' uncertainty about the overall interpretation (fate switch vs selective disruption) affects confidence in the temporal model's mechanistic implications.

Both address the differential sensitivity model and synapse specificity interpretation (C18, C73). OpenEval supports this model based on temperature-shift data. Peer reviewers explicitly reject the synapse specificity interpretation, stating 'the data do not address a "synaptic function" of Notch' and that 'the concept of synapse specificity...is an interpretation that is not directly addressed by the data.'

Overlapping claims about synapse specificity interpretation (C5, C50, C73). OpenEval supports the pathway's role in synapse specificity based on converging evidence. Peer reviewers explicitly reject this interpretation, emphasizing that the data document muscle differentiation rather than synapse specificity and requesting substantial revision of this framing.

OpenEval evaluates established background knowledge (C29-C30, C86) including UNC-40/DCC homology and M lineage origin. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; these represent contextual claims rather than novel findings requiring peer assessment.
